classify_evidences.text: However, the three carpels did not fuse to form a normal stigma, thus preventing pollination and seeds production (Fig.
6f,g). We also investigated the expression activities of KNAT2-like1 in male, female and superior ovary flower buds at various stages by in situ hybridization.

6e). Post anthesis, the k-1 and k-2 mutant flowers continued to grow such that ultimately the ovaries were located above the other floral organs, resulting in bisexual flowers with superior ovaries, similar to those of tomato.

Our findings support a model in which the loss of function of any one of these three genes leads to receptacle arrest and promotes stamen development; however, compared with knat2-like1 mutants, carpel initiation is also repressed in crc and er, resulting in a female-to-male sexual transition (Extended Data Fig. 8j).

Taken together, these findings indicate a key role for KNAT2-like1 in floral receptacle development and inferior ovary formation and suggest a regulatory mechanism involving genetic interaction with ER and CRC.

KNAT2-like1 was specifically expressed in the receptacle; however, besides expression in receptacle after S5, CRC and ER also showed overlapping expression with AG1 during carpel primordia initiation at S4 and S5 (Extended Data Fig. 8i).

The development of male flowers in the k-2 mutants was identical to WT (Extended Data Fig. 7a,c,g), with carpel primordia development arresting after S5 and stamen primordia gradually enlarging until mature pollen formed before anthesis (Extended Data Fig. 7a,c).
In female flowers, the receptacle and carpel continued to grow after S5, and the receptacle grew rapidly and wrapped around the carpel to form the inferior ovary (Extended Data Fig. 7b,d).
Although the superior ovary mutant still has an FIM, the arrested receptacle and upward carpel growth were observed (Fig.

6g). The spatial expression patterns of known abaxial-specific genes, KAN-1, KAN-2 and AFO/FIL47,48, and an adaxial-specific gene, PHAVOLUTA (PHV)49, in normal inferior ovaries and aberrant superior ovaries were consistent with this change in placenta morphology (Extended Data Fig. 7i–k).
